Title:Offline AI Modules: Voice-First Offline Architecture, Hardware Reference Stack, Quantization and Benchmarking
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:The Offline AI Modules workstream enables practical, low-power, and community-accessible deployment of voice-first AI systems that operate fully offline. Designed for African language communities where speech is the dominant mode of interaction and internet connectivity is unreliable or absent, the workstream delivers three reinforcing components: a modular voice-first offline architecture, a low-cost hardware reference bill of materials, and a reproducible quantization and a reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline for instruction-tuned language models in the 2-5B parameter class. This paper presents the first end-to-end benchmark evaluation of the stack across two hardware tiers: an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (TierB) and a Raspberry Pi5 (TierA). Three instruction-tuned models are evaluated across four quantization formats, assessed for deployment metrics (decode throughput, chat latency, memory, power) and multilingual quality (topic classification accuracy on MasakhaNEWS across English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Yoruba; per-language perplexity drift). Speech recognition is evaluated using Ethio-ASR on Amharic and Oromo across both tiers. The principal finding is that Q4_K_M quantization represents the best size-to-quality trade-off for deployment on both tiers: gemma-4-E2B-it achieves 28.8t/s decode throughput and 89.2% topic classification accuracy at Q4_K_M on TierB, while all three models run within the 16GB memory budget on TierA.

report.summary: arXiv paper benchmarks offline voice-first AI stack for African languages, finding Q4_K_M quantization best balances quality and size on Jetson Orin NX and Raspberry Pi 5.
report.background: Many African language communities rely on speech for daily interaction, yet internet connectivity can be unreliable or absent. Cloud-based voice assistants assume stable broadband, raising access, cost, latency, and privacy barriers. Recent small language models in the 2–5B parameter class and edge accelerators make local inference plausible, but developers lack reproducible guidance on hardware, quantization, power, memory, and multilingual quality. This paper addresses that gap by combining a modular voice-first offline architecture, a low-cost hardware bill of materials, and a reproducible quantization and benchmarking pipeline. It evaluates deployment on NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and Raspberry Pi 5 across multiple models, quantization formats, and African languages, aiming to make community-accessible offline voice AI practical.
key_points: The workstream proposes a modular voice-first offline architecture designed for speech-dominant communities where connectivity is unreliable or absent, so voice interaction works entirely on local hardware without cloud dependence.

It defines a low-cost hardware reference stack across two tiers: TierB uses NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, while TierA uses Raspberry Pi 5, with all tested models fitting within a 16GB memory budget on TierA.
Three instruction-tuned models in the 2–5B parameter class are evaluated across four quantization formats. Q4_K_M is reported as the best size-to-quality trade-off for both hardware tiers.
Deployment metrics include decode throughput, chat latency, memory, and power. On TierB, gemma-4-E2B-it reaches 28.8 tokens/s decode and 89.2% topic classification accuracy at Q4_K_M.

Multilingual quality is tested with MasakhaNEWS topic classification across English, Hausa, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Yoruba, plus per-language perplexity drift and Ethio-ASR speech recognition on Amharic and Oromo across both tiers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this paper pushes voice AI toward offline, low-power edge deployment rather than cloud-only pipelines, offering reproducible benchmark data for quantization and hardware choices. Developers gain practical guidance on Q4_K_M as a default format, two concrete hardware tiers, and multilingual evaluation methods for underrepresented languages. Regular users in low-connectivity regions could see cheaper, more private, and more reliable voice interfaces that work without internet. It also strengthens the case for community-accessible AI hardware and localized speech datasets, potentially encouraging more investment in African-language NLP, edge accelerators, and compact instruction-tuned models.
report.tools: Follow llama.cpp and GGUF Q4_K_M quantization, Ollama for local model serving, whisper.cpp for offline speech recognition, and Hugging Face Optimum for quantization workflows. Hardware references include NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and Raspberry Pi 5. Datasets and benchmarks to watch include MasakhaNEWS for multilingual topic classification and Ethio-ASR for Amharic and Oromo speech recognition.
